problem: Existing VLN and zero-shot exploration systems use VLMs only as an add-on to separate mapping and planning pipelines. They need prior maps, pre-captured candidate images, node graphs, or depth/LiDAR/multi-camera sensing, so they are poorly suited to first-time exploration of unknown, dynamic spaces on low-cost robots.
motivation: Search-and-rescue, warehouse and monitoring tasks need robots that can explore and find targets without a pre-mapping phase. Map-traversal baselines (random walk, wall bounce) are inefficient, and path-finding baselines (Bug) need target knowledge. The authors observe that CLIP embeddings alone can supply navigability, familiarity and target cues, so a monocular camera may suffice.
key_idea: Use CLIP as the navigation core: slice each RGB frame into six tiles, score each tile for navigability, familiarity and target confidence by embedding correlation, and feed the scores to a lightweight motion backend that outputs low-level commands directly.
insight: A monocular VLM with contrastive positive/negative prompt correlation is enough for obstacle avoidance and target discovery in real indoor scenes, with no depth or map. The ablations show that look-around is needed for trap recovery (SR drops to 50% without it, with better path length only through survivorship bias). The familiarity memory is needed for efficient exploration (without it the robot oscillates between corners, giving longer paths and lower SR).
method: Frontend tiling: each frame is sliced into 2x3 tiles (NEAR/FAR x LEFT/CENTER/RIGHT) with ~20% overlap, each encoded by the OpenCLIP visual encoder into a 512-d embedding; per-tile pixel standard deviation flags texture-poor tiles.

Navigability/target middleware: tile embeddings are correlated (inner product) with pre-encoded positive and negative text-prompt databases built from a hierarchical YAML prompt template. The score in [-1,1] is the contrast between positive and negative, so no fixed threshold is needed.

Familiarity middleware: a database of visual embeddings of visited places (no images stored), merged by count-based averaging or a rolling average with decay lambda. Familiar tiles are penalized to push the robot toward unexplored areas.

Motion mixer backend: combines navigability, familiarity and std-dev per tile to choose motion (3-DOF omnidirectional). It has three modes: basic navigation, look-around and target lock, where the target has priority over navigable tiles.

Trap detection and look-around: the robot is flagged trapped if it moves <0.2 m in 5 s or the proximity switch halts it. It then rotates 360 degrees, collects nav scores per heading, applies Gaussian smoothing and picks the best heading (with a bonus for deviating from the old heading). Look-around also runs at mission start.

Entropy Preserving Score (EP): a new metric fitted to the random-walk L-R curve of each environment, meant to make exploration efficiency comparable across settings and information levels; SPL is reduced to R * mean inverse path length.

Rover Master UGV and RoboSim2D: a custom omnidirectional platform (Jetson Orin, FLIR RGB camera, 2D LiDAR for safety/visualization only, ~5 FPS with GPU-parallel pipeline) and a 2D simulator built from the LiDAR maps to run baselines.

setting.backbone: OpenCLIP (frozen, CLIP ViT vision + text encoder, D=512) with a hand-designed rule-based motion backend
setting.observation: monocular RGB only (FLIR camera ~30 cm high); IMU heading and odometry from the ESC used for look-around and trap detection; 2D LiDAR only as a safety kill switch
setting.action_space: direct low-level 3-DOF motion commands (forward/sideways/rotation) on an omnidirectional UGV; look-around 360° rotation
setting.simulator: real world (two indoor scenes: warehouse/machine hall and office); baselines run in custom RoboSim2D
setting.privileged: none for VL-Explore (LiDAR used only for safety and offline trajectory evaluation); baselines Bug/WaveFront use known target location or map information

numbers_note: The main aggregate table (Table 4: S.R., P.L., SPL, EP against all baselines) and the ablation figure are not included in the extracted text. The text gives only SPL 0.357 for VL-Explore, compared with VLMnav 0.210 (0.136 without depth) and GOAT 0.64 (0.19 without prior knowledge), reported by those papers on different setups. The per-pair trajectory lengths are in Table 1 of the supplement, but there are no SR/SPL rows per method.
results: In two real indoor scenes, VL-Explore reaches 95% SR in the warehouse and 91.7% in the office with monocular RGB only. It travels far shorter paths than random walk, wall bounce and wave-front (e.g. 8.3 m vs ~150 m for the same task), and its SPL is comparable to Bug path-finding that knows the target. The paper reports 0.357 SPL without depth or memory, but the comparison to VLMnav and GOAT is not on the same benchmark.
limitations: Fails on texture-less or transparent surfaces (blank walls, water tank), in open spaces without visual cues, and in artificial cardboard mazes; narrow gaps (~50 cm) are treated as blocked by the fixed tile slicing.
The familiarity database saturates in long missions; only one simple target (a toy bear) and two scenes were tested, with a fixed hand-crafted rule-based backend and no language instructions.
Comparison to SOTA VLN systems is only qualitative or across incompatible setups; the custom EP metric and the baselines in a custom 2D simulator are not standard benchmarks.
